direction: Write about someone others rely on to find a way through the countryside. Start with a small task on a walk, then show how they learned the route. Keep the wish to recover the fields in the background. Two sentences; straightforward and confident.

Write about a furniture maker who is tired of hearing their grandfather's land story. Give it a little everyday irritation or humor. They still care about getting the home back, but have customers and bills to think about. Start with work, not childhood. Two or three sentences.

Keep this almost bare: an assistant is asked to sign a false survey and refuses. Show the immediate cost. Leave out a speech about principle or a sentence explaining their personality. Three short sentences, with the refusal at the centre.

Write about the cost and annoyance of sending letters nobody answers. Focus on a small decision about money or postage, not the grand failure of justice. Let the person sound fed up. Three sentences with different lengths.

Tell a brief incident: sheep need food, a fence blocks the grazing, the shepherd acts. The urgency comes from caring for animals. Start with the flock or the fence. One or two sentences, moving quickly.

Make this warm and sociable. The person gets meals and seasonal work because they keep up with neighbors, not because they are destined to defend ancestral land. Begin with someone welcoming them back. Two sentences.

Treat this as an ordinary pay-and-supply calculation. The quartermaster wants the garrison fed and wages sent home. Show what they take and who loses out, with no speech about being heartless. One longer sentence plus one short sentence.

Make this about a parent's expectations. The officer uses their father's maps because disagreeing with him would be difficult. A short line of remembered advice is allowed. Three sentences; family pressure matters more than military grandeur.

Tell a practical mistake in road planning. The engineer trusts a map, sends crews, and discovers why locals objected. They may be embarrassed rather than malicious. Start with the plan going wrong. Two sentences.

Make this a selfish career decision. The administrator wants a better posting and rushes work to impress headquarters. Use a concrete deadline or report, no general lesson about ambition. Two sentences.

Write about a tired officer who has learned how to avoid a confrontation. Show the small thing they do when a crowd blocks surveyors. They want work finished with less shouting. Start with the crowd. Two or three sentences.

Show a rule causing an awkward encounter, preferably with someone the officer knows. They insist on paperwork the person cannot obtain. Let the exchange show their rigid habits; do not explain that bureaucracy is cruel. Three short sentences.

Write about a teacher doing a small kindness for one absent pupil after road restrictions. Give us the visit or lesson, not a statement about responsibility. Start with the pupil being missing from class. Two sentences.

Use a child's ordinary memory of the agreement ceremony: being lifted up, a parent explaining, wanting to see the crowd. Then a later encounter with guards changes what the person believes. A simple wish to visit family can remain. Two or three sentences.

Make this an awkward but slightly funny family conversation. The father wants to debate the agreement; the bicycle repairer would rather discuss a broken wheel or finish work. Work and avoidance should matter more than a heroic claim about smaller roads. Three sentences.

Make the clerk's departure partly self-protection. A boss wants altered records signed in their name; they leave before being blamed. Give one useful fact about the old office. Avoid making this another noble survey refusal. Two sentences.

Write about a modest plan the tailor keeps putting off: a visit, a sales trip, or seeing family. Road closures make planning difficult. Keep politics in the background. Two sentences, gentle and ordinary.

Make this friendly and observant. The water carrier has routine conversations with guards, and knows when someone is relieved or goes for food. Then a permit change ends the work. Start with a remembered bit of the routine. Two sentences.

Show the officer encountering their own rules when an aunt's visit is blocked. They had ignored complaints before; now they want an exception. Leave the reader to notice the unfairness. A short quoted reply is allowed. Three sentences.

Write about why someone wants to keep a comfortable posting. The roads are blocked, but their aunt's shop has soldiers buying supplies. The person likes the arrangement. Keep it matter-of-fact and mildly self-satisfied. Two sentences.

Make this about a small office success the character is proud of: a changed form wins praise and makes life harder for travelers. Use what they did, not a label such as 'institutional coercion'. One sentence can carry the whole incident if clear.

Describe an uneven daily routine: familiar drivers get a nod, strangers get every bag checked. The officer likes recognising people and keeping a quiet shift. No concluding sentence interpreting that habit. Two sentences.

Tell a short encounter. A visitor points out that a valid permit was refused; the officer unfolds the old agreement and repeats their answer. One short quote is allowed. Make the reason for the argument understandable. Three sentences.

Write about homesickness. The officer keeps asking for a transfer and missing family events. They still do the job while waiting. The feeling should come from one ordinary detail, not 'an unpaid debt'. Two or three sentences.

Make the radio repairer curious about how things work. Remembering veterans is secondary to fixing an old set or trying a repair. They had little weapons training before joining. Start with the equipment. Two sentences.

Write about the uncomfortable relationship with the uncle who came back. The other uncle did not return; questions at home go unanswered. No dramatic gesture about being unable to sit down. Two sentences, quiet and direct.

Keep the child's escape memory oddly ordinary: the orchard path, a lost shoe, being hungry, or wanting to go back for something. Choose one. Later they recognise the route. Avoid making the orchard a symbol of the entire war. Two or three sentences.

Write about unglamorous work after the fighting: checking spellings, knocking on doors, crossing out the name of someone found alive. The shop worker helps neighbors look for missing relatives. Show a small task. Three short sentences.

Keep this about a family conversation that never quite happens. The mother will not describe her escape; neighbors tell bits of it. The person tries to ask at a bad moment and leaves it alone. Avoid turning the lack of shoes into a perfect reason to become a shoemaker. Two or three sentences.

Make this about eagerness and embarrassment at a defense drill. The person was too young during the old fighting and now tries too hard to prove useful. Let an older volunteer correct something simple. A little humor is fine. Three sentences.
Show a hurried report and a choice to avoid checking it. The officer is more interested in closing the inquiry than visiting damaged streets. Keep the deception concrete. Two sentences.

Contrast what the officer actually remembers with what they wrote, using plain facts. Wet boots and confused orders are enough; no statement about truth or memory. Start with the memory. Two sentences.

Make this grief with no revenge speech. The officer asks to be posted near the place where their brother died, but still struggles to answer a family letter. One small hesitation is enough. Two sentences.

Write about a person applying their usual work habits in the wrong setting. They measure road damage and order repairs while residents wait to ask about homes. They want the next inspection to go well. Two sentences.

Make the officer proud of a medal and embarrassed by what the citation leaves out. Give the clear reason the column was delayed, then what they say when asked. No numbered battle day or relief claim. Three sentences.

Describe a dull training lesson that becomes uncomfortable when a recruit asks about residents in the photographs. The officer keeps talking about convoy spacing. Use an ordinary classroom action, not a philosophical ending. Two or three sentences.
